meta.description: Douglas Adams didn't write it. The joke has been in print since an 1853 magazine anecdote, and Quote Investigator found no match in his works.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It's not the fall that kills you; it's the sudden stop at the end'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Adams. Quote Investigator traces this quip to an 1853 anecdote and found no solid match in his writings — here is the dated chronology.

answer.label: Not Douglas Adams — an anonymous joke, in print since 1853
answer.authorDates: Anonymous quip · documented in print from October 1853
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator traces this quip to an anecdote printed in The Ladies’ Repository in October 1853 and states that it “has not found any solid matches for this quip in the writings of Douglas Adams.” The phrasing drifted through a dozen retellings before the internet handed it to him; no author of the modern sentence has ever been identified.

source.heading: Where the joke actually starts

docMeta.dd: Anonymous joke family; Quote Investigator tentatively credits the anecdote’s Charlie Bates
2010 — a chapter epigraph in Guerrilla Project Management

source.excerpt: After a late supper, and two or three extra glasses, Charlie Bates is apt to be somnambulistic. Night before last, being an occasion of this kind, he backed himself out of his chamber window and fell to the pavement, a distance of ten or twelve feet. A passer-by came up to condole with him, remarking, “You seem to have had a bad fall.” “My dear sir,” answered Charlie, “the fall was a trifle not worth mentioning; but the sudden stop was decidedly unpleasant.”
trail: The joke is in print long before Adams. Quote Investigator traces the family to an October 1853 anecdote in The Ladies’ Repository, in which a man who has backed out of his bedroom window tells a passer-by that the fall was a trifle but the sudden stop was decidedly unpleasant. Adams was born in 1952.

The wording closest to today’s is anonymous. QI records the November 1893 Locomotive Firemen’s Magazine printing it with an anonymous attribution: not the height of the fall that hurt him, but the sudden stop at the end of it.

Adams’s own falling joke is a different one. QI notes that Life, the Universe and Everything (1982) has the knack of flying — “throw yourself at the ground and miss” — and says it found no solid match for this quip anywhere in his writings.
It is not on his Wikiquote page either. Wikiquote’s Douglas Adams entry runs to three sections — Quotes, Quotes about Adams, External links — and the phrase appears in none of them.
source.excerptNote: This is the ancestor, not the sentence. The modern wording — “kills you,” “at the end” — assembled itself gradually across the following century, and no author of it has ever been identified.

source.rightsNote: The 1853 anecdote above is long out of copyright, but it is not the sentence people quote. The exact modern wording has no identified author and no traceable first publication, so no rights status can honestly be asserted for it. The 2010 book that prints it under Adams’s name is in copyright, but plainly did not originate the line.

author.name: Douglas Adams
author.kicker: The name it gets pinned on
author.heading: So why Douglas Adams?
author.bio: Douglas Adams was an English author, humourist and screenwriter, best known for The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy (novel, 1979) and its sequels, among them Life, the Universe and Everything (1982). He is also one of the internet’s most dependable magnets for lines he never wrote, and his Wikiquote page carries no Misattributed section at all — so a quip like this one circulates under his name with nothing standing in its way. The falling joke he actually told is the better one: that the knack of flying lies in learning to throw yourself at the ground and miss.

copyAttribution: Not Douglas Adams. "It's not the fall that kills you; it's the sudden stop at the end" is an anonymous joke. Quote Investigator found no solid match for it in Adams's writings and traces the family of quips to an anecdote printed in The Ladies' Repository, New York, in October 1853, in which a man who has fallen from a window says the fall was a trifle not worth mentioning but the sudden stop was decidedly unpleasant. The earliest citation crediting Adams that Quote Investigator records is a 2010 chapter epigraph, published after his death. misattribution.heading: Three famous names, one anonymous joke
misattribution.intro: Quote Investigator’s framing is precise and worth keeping: Douglas Adams, Spike Milligan and Terry Pratchett have each received credit for telling jokes in this family. That is not the same as any of them writing this sentence, and only one of the three has ever been handed this exact wording.

items.why: Quote Investigator says it “has not found any solid matches for this quip in the writings of Douglas Adams,” and the earliest Adams-credited instance in its chronology is a chapter epigraph in a 2010 project-management book — published after his death. Goodreads still carries the line under his name with no book or source named.

items.scope: A cousin joke, not this one
items.why: The Milligan credit in QI’s chronology comes from a 1998 novel recalling him on television saying that flying isn’t dangerous — crashing is. Same idea, different sentence, and reported at second hand.
In Sourcery (1988), as QI documents, Rincewind protests that he is afraid not of heights but of grounds. That is Pratchett’s own joke in the same family — it is not this quip.

misattribution.truthLine: The line belongs to nobody famous. Quote Investigator tentatively credits the 1853 anecdote about a somnambulant Charlie Bates with starting the family, and every version since — 1883, 1893, 1922, 1945, 1960 — is another retelling as the phrasing drifted toward the form we use today.

context.heading: A joke that kept finding new things to be afraid of
lead: Falling jokes are a genre, and this is the genre’s most durable line. Quote Investigator’s chronology shows the same gag re-tooled for whatever happened to be frightening people: a drunk backing out of a bedroom window in 1853, railway braking in 1893, the new flying machines in 1911, motor cars in 1922, aviation again in 1945. By the time it reached the internet the machinery had fallen away and only the punchline was left — which is precisely the condition in which a quote goes looking for a famous owner.

Adams is a natural host. He wrote what is probably the best-known joke in English about hitting the ground, so a stray line about sudden stops slots into his voice without friction. That is the whole trap: this is a quote that sounds like him rather than a quote that is his, and the two are very hard to tell apart at the speed people share things.
context.detailsSummary: How the wording drifted into its modern shape
detailsBody: By 1893 the sentence had nearly arrived. The Locomotive Firemen’s Magazine printed it with an anonymous attribution, as the view of a man who declared it was not the height of the fall that hurt him but the sudden stop at the end of it. The remaining drift was toward violence: Popular Science in 1945 had speed rather than the fall, and killing rather than hurting, and Harry Harrison’s 1960 story in Analog compressed the two into the modern rhythm — speed never hurt anybody, it’s the sudden stop at the end.

What no citation supplies is the moment somebody put Adams’s name on it. The earliest Adams-credited instance in Quote Investigator’s chronology is a chapter epigraph in Kenneth T. Hanley’s Guerrilla Project Management (2010), which prints the line exactly as it circulates today and credits him with no source. QI presents its list as selected citations rather than an exhaustive sweep, so the credit was very likely already in circulation before that book picked it up.
context.pull: … it was not the height of the fall that hurt him, but the sudden stop at the end of it. — anonymous, 1893

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's article "Quip Origin: It's Not the Fall That Hurts You; It's the Sudden Stop at the End" (25 March 2025) states it "has not found any solid matches for this quip in the writings of Douglas Adams," and tentatively credits Charlie Bates with originating the family of quips based on an anecdote printed in October 1853 in The Ladies' Repository, New York, pages 471-472.

The same QI article documents the November 1893 Locomotive Firemen's Magazine (Terre Haute, Indiana) instance with an anonymous attribution — "it was not the height of the fall that hurt him, but the sudden stop at the end of it" — plus instances in 1883, 1903, 1911, 1922, 1945 (Popular Science, speed/kills) and 1960 (Harry Harrison in Analog, "Speed never hurt anybody—it's the sudden stop at the end").

The same QI article states that Douglas Adams's Life, the Universe and Everything (1982, chapter 11) contains a thematically related but different flying joke — the knack of flying is learning how to throw yourself at the ground and miss — and that the earliest instance in its chronology crediting Adams with this quip is a chapter epigraph in Kenneth T. Hanley's Guerrilla Project Management (2010). It also records Terry Pratchett's Sourcery (1988) grounds joke and a 1998 novel crediting Spike Milligan with the flying/crashing joke.

Wikiquote's Douglas Adams page has only three top-level sections (Quotes; Quotes about Adams; External links), carries no Misattributed, Disputed or Attributed section, and the phrases "sudden stop" and "not the fall that kills you" do not appear anywhere on it.

Douglas Adams was born 11 March 1952 and died 11 May 2001; he was English, described as an author, humourist and screenwriter; The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy novel was published in 1979 and Life, the Universe and Everything in 1982.
This Google Books record is the volume Quote Investigator links for its 1853 citation: The Ladies' Repository, Volume 13.
Goodreads displays the exact wording "It's not the fall that kills you; it's the sudden stop at the end." attributed to Douglas Adams, and names no book or source for it.

Quote Investigator's separate article on the related falling joke — the optimist who says "All's well so far" while passing each storey — traces it to an 1887 item in the French newspaper Le Figaro and finds no single identifiable originator.
